{{Short description|Original name of the FLLA World Cup, contested 1656–1684}}
The '''Ayuman Cup''', styled at its inaugural edition as the '''Ayuman Continental Tournament''', was an international [[Arraby]] competition contested by the senior men's national teams of the leading Ayuman football associations. It was the original form of what is now the '''[[FLLA World Cup]]''', and the name the competition bore from its first edition in 1656 until it was relaunched and renamed at the [[1700 FLLA World Cup|1700 edition]], following the constitution of the [[FLLA]] and its seven continental confederations. All entrants in the Ayuman Cup era were drawn from [[Ayuma]], the confederations not yet existing.<ref name="names">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/history/early-competition-names|title=From the Ayuman Cup to the FLLA World Cup: the early names of the competition|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=12 February 1764}}</ref>

Seven editions were completed between 1656 and 1684. An eighth, the [[1664 FLLA World Cup|1664 tournament]], was awarded but abandoned before play on the outbreak of the [[Great Imperial War]], and the editions scheduled for 1688, 1692 and 1696 were all cancelled because of the [[Red War]] and the subsequent reconstruction. When the competition resumed at the [[1700 FLLA World Cup|1700 edition]] it did so under its modern name, making 1684 the last tournament staged as the Ayuman Cup.<ref name="names" />

[[Lycroa]] were the most successful side of the era, winning three of the seven titles. The competition was marked by a steady fall in scoring across its editions, from an average of 6.15 goals per match at the high-scoring inaugural tournament of 1656 to 2.75 per match by 1684, and by a gradual expansion of the field from nine entrants in 1656 to sixteen in 1684.

==Format==
The Ayuman Cup was organised by an informal congress of the Ayuman national associations, the body that ran the competition before the foundation of the [[FLLA]]. Each edition combined a group stage, contested on a single round-robin basis under the two-points-for-a-win system then in use, with a knockout stage of semi-finals, a third-place playoff and a final. Knockout ties were played over 90 minutes and, where level, extended by a single 30-minute period of [[wikipedia:Extra time|extra time]]. The [[wikipedia:Penalty shoot-out (association football)|penalty shoot-out]] had not yet been introduced: a tie still level after extra time was settled by a replay, or, under the regulations applied in 1680, by lot. The provision was invoked only once in a final, in 1680, when [[Lycroa]] took the title on the toss of a coin after a goalless draw with [[Eldjo]].<ref name="overview-1680">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1680/final|title=The 1680 Ayuman Cup final: Lycroa 0–0 Eldjo, decided by coin toss|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=9 June 1763}}</ref>

The hosts won the title on three occasions, [[Emara]] in 1672, [[Lycroa]] in 1680 and [[Alzuria]] in 1684; [[Alzuria]]'s victory on home soil at the final Ayuman Cup was the only major title the [[Alzurian Union|union]] would win.

==Trophies==
Two rotating trophies were contested during the Ayuman Cup era. The original prize was the '''[[FLLA World Cup#The Ayuma Cup|Ayuma Cup]]''', introduced at the inaugural 1656 edition and presented to the champions of 1656 and 1660. It was retired in 1668 and carried back to [[Lycroa]] by the 1660 champions, who as its last holders retained it; the Ayuma Cup survives in a museum collection.<ref name="ayuma-cup">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/trophies/the-ayuma-cup|title=The Ayuma Cup and its early history|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=2 July 1764}}</ref>

From 1668 the champions received the original '''[[FLLA World Cup#The Andah Cup|Andah Cup]]''', which passed to the winner of each tournament through to 1684. After [[Alzuria]]'s win that year the cup remained in the [[Alzurian Union|union]], where it was destroyed in 1688 at the outbreak of the [[Red War]]. No bespoke permanent trophy yet existed; the permanent-trophy tradition that has since characterised the competition began only with the commissioning of a new prize for the [[1700 FLLA World Cup|1700 edition]].<ref name="andah-cup">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/trophies/the-andah-cup|title=The original Andah Cup, 1656 to 1688|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=2 July 1764}}</ref>

==Goalscoring==
Scoring in the Ayuman Cup fell steadily across its seven editions, from 6.15 goals per match in 1656 to 2.75 per match in 1684, as defensive organisation developed and the field expanded. The highest individual return of the era was the 15 goals scored by [[Estijan|Estijani]] forward Tomas Brody at the inaugural tournament in 1656, a tally no later top scorer of the period approached.<ref name="overview-1656">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1656/overview|title=The 1656 Ayuman Cup: tournament overview|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=14 March 1763}}</ref>
